top_choice_rationale: Kiyotaki and Moore (P003) identified one specific mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. The mechanism is about three decades old and has been tested through theory, quantitative work and post-2008 policy analysis. The credit rests on one two-author contribution with no obvious missing claimant, and I treat that as a practical advantage, not as merit in itself. It is distinct from the 2022 prize on bank runs and deposit insurance, because it needs no run or intermediary failure, and a citation should say so explicitly. I concede that empirical identification of collateral channels is weaker than the theory and that the work is narrower than the alternatives. P001 (Melitz and Helpman) is a close second. It has the stronger record of repeated firm-level testing, but its second name is open to question because Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are not credited. P002 (Calvo, Taylor and Woodford) has the largest policy footprint, but the credit is spread over eight names and the trio depends on how the discovery is defined. I rank any award above no award. I have not independently verified citation or priority details.
recusal_note: No connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz, Helpman, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford is apparent from my profile. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and an IIES colleague of both. Neither is a candidate in any proposal, but Krusell shares my first choice, so that agreement is not independent. My long-running collaboration with Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li concerns work not on this shortlist. My proximity to growth and firm-dynamics research may affect how I weigh P001. I disclose these ties without adjudicating them and have completed the ballot.
